papers.title: Development and validation of a predictive model for assisted walking in Multiple System Atrophy: a multicenter bidirectional cohort study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and validate machine learning-based predictive prognostic models for assisted walking in patients with Multiple System Atrophy (MSA). METHODS: This was a multicenter bidirectional cohort study involving 173 patients with MSA (training set: 122; validation set: 51) from three hospitals (May 2022-January 2025). Baseline data (demographics, clinical manifestations, imaging, neurofunctional assessments) were collected, with follow-up until assisted walking occurrence. We constructed Cox regression and five machine learning prognostic models, which were evaluated via C-index, AUC, calibration curves, DCA, and K-M curves (Epidata, SPSS 25.0, R v4.2.2). RESULTS: 68.97% of patients required assisted walking (median: 48 months). Patients with MSA-C exhibited higher assisted walking proportion (75% vs 60.27%, P < 0.05) and shorter median time (47 vs 49 months, P = 0.042) than patients with MSA-P. Cox and CoxBoost models (incorporating six predictors) had training/validation C-indexes of 0.878/0.749 and 0.875/0.748, respectively, with stable AUC and good calibration. INTERPRETATION: MSA-P and MSA-C have distinct clinical features. The six identified predictors influence assisted walking outcomes. With acceptable stability and accuracy, the Cox and CoxBoost models exhibit promising prognostic performance of patients with MSA.

papers.title: A four-year longitudinal study on the acute and chronic DBS neuromodulation effects in Parkinson's disease.
Pain in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder: Findings from longitudinal and deep-phenotyping cohorts.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pain is a common non-motor symptom in Parkinson's disease, yet whether it emerges in the prodromal period and whether it reflects underlying dopaminergic degeneration remains poorly characterized. OBJECTIVES: Our objectives are threefold: to determine whether pain is elevated in polysomnogram-confirmed isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), whether it predicts phenoconversion to overt synucleinopathy, and whether it is associated with regional dopaminergic deficits. METHODS: Participants with iRBD (n = 507) and demographically-matched controls (n = 33) enrolled in the North American Prodromal Synucleinopathy (NAPS) Consortium from August 2018 through July 31, 2025 were analyzed. Pain was assessed using MDS-UPDRS item 1.9. Cox proportional hazards models - including a time-varying model incorporating repeated assessments - examined pain as a predictor of phenoconversion. Dopamine transporter (DAT) SPECT imaging was performed in a subset (n = 244), and ordinal logistic regression models evaluated associations between regional striatal binding ratios and pain severity. An independently recruited clinically enriched chronic pain cohort (n = 110) with and without RBD underwent detailed pain phenotyping without neuroimaging. RESULTS: Participants with iRBD had significantly higher odds of greater pain severity than controls (OR = 2.24, 95%CI 1.17-4.49, p = 0.02). Moderate-severe baseline pain predicted phenoconversion (HR = 2.21, 95%CI 1.13-4.32, p = 0.02), an estimate that remained stable after adjustment for several medical covariates, although the overall three-category model was not statistically significant (p = 0.08). Cross-sectional striatal DAT binding was not associated with symptom severity. Despite greater subjective pain burden, objective pressure algometry did not differ between iRBD and controls. papers.title: Fluvoxamine exerts neurorestorative effects via the Sigma-1 receptor in two mouse models of dopaminergic degeneration.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
papers.abstract: The selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor fluvoxamine has high binding affinity for the Sigma-1 receptor, an intracellular chaperone protein modulating neuroplasticity and pro-survival pathways. We set out to examine the effects of fluvoxamine in mouse models of dopaminergic degeneration driven by neurotoxin-induced damage or seeded alpha-synuclein aggregation. In mice with unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine lesions, five weeks of daily treatment with fluvoxamine at the doses of 0.3 or 20 mg/kg/day gradually restored contralateral forelimb use and partially protected nigral dopaminergic neurons while reducing the number of phagocytically activated microglia. In addition, the larger dose significantly increased the density of dopaminergic fibers in the dopamine-depleted striatum. These beneficial effects were absent in Sigma-1 receptor knockout mice. We next evaluated the 20 mg/kg dose in mice inoculated with preformed alpha-synuclein fibrils in the striatum, starting treatment one month post-surgery and administering it daily for four months. Although fluvoxamine did not alter the formation of alpha-synuclein inclusions, it promoted a regenerative response in the nigrostriatal pathway, increasing dopaminergic fiber density in the depleted striatum and markedly reducing the number of activated microglia in the substantia nigra. The results from both parkinsonian models demonstrate that fluvoxamine treatment stimulates fiber regrowth in the damaged nigrostriatal system while inhibiting microglial overactivation. These findings support Sigma-1 receptors as a potential target for disease-modifying therapies in Parkinson's disease and point to fluvoxamine as a relevant repurposing candidate.

papers.title: Decoding neurodegeneration: RNA therapeutics in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease are of major global health concern considering that they are progressive and not curable. The standard therapeutic methods mainly aim at the treatment of the symptoms, and they do not treat the molecular processes that contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease. Over the last few years, RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as a promising approach to precisely target disease-specific genes and pathways at the molecular level. This review examines the involvement of the use of different RNA-based methods such as small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA (miRNA), messenger RNA (mRNA) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in the management of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. The article emphasises the ability of these therapies to regulate gene expression that relates to some of the major pathological phenotypes, including amyloid-beta deposition, hyperphosphorylation of the tau protein, and alpha-synuclein aggregation. In addition to that, it also talks about the progress in delivery systems to address limitations such as the blood-brain barrier, making RNA therapeutics more clinically applicable. The existing evidence of research shows that there is great potential to slow the progression of disease and improve the functioning of neurons. In spite of these developments, there are still some issues such as the problems of stability, off-target effects, and mass production. On the whole, RNA-based therapeutics is an innovative solution that can potentially turn the face of neurodegenerative diseases treatment. These innovations should be translated to effective therapeutic interventions, which can only be achieved through further research and clinical validation.

papers.title: AI-Based Monitoring Devices for the Identification of Circadian Parameters as Digital Predictive Biomarkers of Neurodegenerative Diseases in Older Adults: Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and related dementias are a growing health burden among older adults. Circadian disruption is increasingly recognized as both a consequence and a potential early marker of neurodegenerative progression. Wearable sensing combined with AI enables continuous, noninvasive, and ecologically valid monitoring of circadian parameters as potential digital biomarkers. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI-enhanced wearable and objective sensing devices used to monitor circadian parameters in older and cognitively vulnerable adults and evaluates their potential as digital predictive biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. METHODS: Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines, an original search of PubMed, Scopus, and JMIR journals (June 2025) yielded 12 studies, 7 of which met updated eligibility criteria on rescreening. A complementary search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library (March 24, 2026) added 3 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references (excluded records retained to delimit the corpus boundary). Two reviewers (JMH-Z and JM-R) independently assessed risk of bias with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Heterogeneous end points precluded meta-analysis; the narrative synthesis covered 4 prespecified domains: device class, circadian construct, AI and machine learning (ML) method family, and population and neurocognitive context. RESULTS: The final corpus comprised 13 records (10 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references) published from 2015 to 2025. Wrist actigraphy predominated, and samples ranged from community-dwelling older adults to nursing home residents with advanced dementia (n=16-7297). papers.title: α-Synuclein Seeding Assay Using Cultured Cells.
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein, a presynaptic protein, is involved in synaptic vesicle dynamics in response to neuronal activity. Mutations of the α-synuclein gene and the neuronal deposition of α-synuclein, called Lewy bodies, are linked to the development of Parkinson's disease. α-Synuclein has a prion-like property that converts its physiological protein conformation to a pathogenic one, forming disease-causing fibrils. Aggregation of these fibrils and subsequent inclusion formation are suggested to interfere with vesicular trafficking and organelle function in neurons. Thus, detection of a prion-like property of α-synuclein and the evaluation of its modifying factors are required to understand the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease and to develop new therapies. In this chapter, we describe a cell-based assay for detecting α-synuclein propagation.

papers.title: Thioredoxin-1 induces immune tolerance against α-syn presented by MHC-II in microglia via promoting Tregs differentiation in MPTP-induced Parkinson's disease mice.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease characterized by the loss of dopaminergic (DAergic) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and the formation of Lewy bodies composed of misfolded alpha-synuclein (α-syn). A growing number of studies indicate that microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and autoimmune responses are important pathological features of PD. Thioredoxin-1 (Trx-1), a multifunctional redox-regulatory protein, exerts neuroprotective effects in 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced PD models, but its impact on microglia-mediated autoimmune responses in PD remains unexplored. In the present study, we demonstrated that Trx-1 suppressed microglial accumulation and the increase of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Furthermore, Trx-1 suppressed the increase of α-syn and major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC-II)-mediated antigen presentation in microglia induced by MPTP. Additionally, MPTP promoted T helper 17 (Th17) cell differentiation, inhibited forkhead box P3 (FOXP3) protein level and regulatory T (Treg) cell differentiation, and enhanced forkhead box O1 (FOXO1) phosphorylation and nuclear exclusion in the SNpc. All these pathological alterations induced by MPTP were effectively restored by Trx-1 overexpression. Our findings highlight the pivotal role of Trx-1 in microglia-mediated autoimmune responses, thereby providing a potential therapeutic target for PD.

papers.title: Modulation of lincRNA-p21/mitomiR-181 and mitomiR-23b/SIRT1 signaling pathways in rotenone-induced neurodegeneration rat model.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss and α-synuclein-rich Lewy body accumulation. Mitochondrial dysfunction and microRNA (miRNA) dysregulation, particularly mitochondrial miRNAs (mitomiRs), are critical drivers of PD pathogenesis. METHODS: This study investigated the neuroprotective efficacy of the SGLT2 inhibitor, dapagliflozin, against rotenone-induced neurotoxicity, focusing on the lincRNA-p21/mitomiR-181/PTEN and mitomiR-23b/SIRT1/AMPK signaling axes. Male Wistar rats were randomized into three groups: a control group, a PD model group received rotenone (2 mg/kg every 48 h, s.c.), and a treatment group received rotenone plus dapagliflozin (10 mg/kg/day, p.o.) for 28 days. RESULTS: In the inducted rotenone group lincRNA-p21 sponges mir-181 which leads to the upregulation of PTEN which inhibits the conversion of PIP2 to PIP3 thus downregulating AKT expression and subsequent activation of GSK-3β kinase enzyme which increases α-synuclein accumulation. In addition, the PD-control group showed upregulation of Mitomir-23b with subsequent downregulation of SIRT-1 expression and inactivation of LKB1. Accompanied by inhibition of AMPK phosphorylation which in turn prevents the degradation of accumulated α-synuclein. Dapagliflozin treatment upregulates mir-181 and downregulates mitomir-23b, which restores DJ-1 levels, which in turn activate the antioxidant genes HO-1 and PINK1, and improve mitochondrial function. CONCLUSIONS: Dapagliflozin exerts neuroprotection by restoring lincRNA-p21/mitomiR-181/PTEN and mitomiR-23b/SIRT1/AMPK homeostasis, thereby inhibiting α-synuclein proteotoxicity and mitigating oxidative stress and neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Gait and Balance Disorders in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Falls in older adults are often the result of gait and balance disorders. These disorders affect a patient's quality of life, reduce their functional capacity, and increase morbidity and mortality. Common conditions in older adults, including arthritis and sarcopenia, contribute to these mobility disorders, but primary care physicians should also consider less common causes, such as neurodegenerative disorders (eg, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease) and normal pressure hydrocephalus. Physicians caring for older adults should ask patients about unsteadiness and falls at every health maintenance visit. Gait should be observed if there is a higher risk for falls based on patient or caregiver concerns. Several mobility assessments can be used to assess fall risk and gait disorders, including the Timed Up and Go test, the 30-Second Chair Stand test, and the 4-Stage Balance test. Fall prevention should include a multifactorial evaluation and individualized intervention strategies. Effective fall prevention involves increasing physical activity, using appropriate assistive devices, and strength training, ideally with physical or occupational therapy.

papers.title: LRRK2 in Focus: A Global Browser Linking Genetic Diversity to Functional Effects.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: LRRK2 (leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) variants are major contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD). Many pathogenic variants increase kinase activity, underscoring the value of functional assays in nominating therapeutic targets such as kinase inhibitors. OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to develop an interactive resource that provides functional context and ancestry-specific variant frequencies. METHODS: Genetic data were analyzed for 116,923 individuals (71,905 PD, 45,018 controls) from the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2) and integrated with clinical and in vitro biochemical kinase activity information. RESULTS: The LRRK2 Browser (http://gp2.org/lrrk2browser) displays genetic data for 22,172 LRRK2 variants (1031 exonic, 12 disease-associated) across 11 populations and functional data for 179 variants. Clinical annotations include age, age at onset, and family history of PD. CONCLUSIONS: The publicly available LRRK2 Browser represents an open-access resource to support LRRK2 variant interpretation. It aims to enhance the translational potential of genetic and functional data for precision medicine and the implementation of gene-targeted therapies in diverse populations. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: Diagnostic Yield of Genetic Testing in Adults with Ataxia: a Decade of Experience at the Johns Hopkins Ataxia Center.
papers.abstract: This retrospective study describes the diagnostic yield of genetic testing in adults with ataxia who were evaluated at the Johns Hopkins Ataxia Center from 2014 to 2024. The Johns Hopkins Ataxia Center (JHAC) outlined a comprehensive genetic testing algorithm for completing genetic testing in 2014, which has been revised over time to reflect updates in the field. Most recently, genome sequencing, with the ability to detect repeat expansions, is recommended as the first-line genetic test in the absence of a known familial pathogenic variant. Electronic medical records of all adult patients who completed genetic counseling at the JHAC from 2014 to 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Data extraction included: 1) clinical data pertaining to ataxia diagnosis and phenotype, including standardized ratings scales (i.e., Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia [SARA] and Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA]), age of symptom onset, and presence of family history; 2) diagnostic genetic tests ordered and resulted; and 3) demographic information, including self-reported biological sex, race and ethnicity, and education level. Of the 750 patients referred for genetic counseling at the JHAC during this time, 510 underwent genetic testing as part of their workup. A total of 204 (40%) of patients received a genetic diagnosis. The most frequently identified genetic diagnosis in our cohort was SCA27B, accounting for 32 probands (14.7% of cohort). The second most frequently identified genetic diagnosis was SCA6 in 25 probands (12.3% of cohort). Individuals with a family history of ataxia were 3.47 times more likely to receive a genetic diagnosis. Individuals with vestibular dysfunction were 1.54 times more likely to receive a genetic diagnosis.
